verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, of David, to make remembrance.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster. Of David. A prayer that makes itself a memorial, a cry that the LORD would remember.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the title the singers read before they sing, and the actor should not skip it: it tells the room who holds the song and what it is for. 'To the choirmaster' hands the psalm to the temple's musical leadership, the person who set the melody and the order of voices. The KJV's 'a Psalm of David' is its own filling in; the Hebrew has only 'of David', which can mean written by him, for him, or in his tradition.

Lehazkir, 'to make remembrance', is the key term, and the KJV 'to bring to remembrance' is accurate but vague about who remembers whom. The verb is the same one used for the memorial portion of an offering, and for the act of invoking a name before God. Either the singer prompts God to remember him (Rashi) or the song itself is a petition to hurry (Metzudat David). Play it as a man jogging the memory of someone he trusts but fears is distracted.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil infinitive of zkr, 'to cause to remember, to invoke'. In the psalm headings it names the purpose of the prayer: to call God's attention to the speaker. Rashi takes it as a language of prayer, comparing 'in the name of the LORD our God we invoke' (Ps 20:8) and 1 Chr 16:4.
A Piel participle with the article, 'the one who leads, the choirmaster' (so Targum 'to praise'); the exact duty is not certain. The same heading stands over many psalms.

verses.translation_literal: God, to deliver me; YHWH, to my help, hasten.
verses.translation_dramatic: God. To rescue me. LORD, to my help, hurry!
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker has no breath for a full sentence. The first line has no verb at all: 'God, to deliver me', and only the last word, chushah, 'hasten!', arrives to carry both lines. The KJV repairs the grammar by putting 'Make haste' twice, and in doing so smooths over the very thing the Hebrew does, which is a man whose syntax collapses under panic. Radak and Meiri both point out that the final imperative reaches back to both halves. Direct the actor to hold the word 'God' and the word 'LORD' as separate calls, and save the command for the end.

The verse also shows the name of God changing. Elohim, the general word, opens the first line, then YHWH, the covenant name, opens the second. This is the plan of this whole psalm, which is built from the end of Psalm 40 with the name Elohim worked into it. For an ancient listener, 'help' here is not comfort but military and legal relief: someone arriving with force to break a siege or a grip. 'Hasten' (chush) is a word of speed, not a request for a favour.

philological_notes.note: Imperative of chush, 'to hurry', with the paragogic -ah that sharpens a command. A single instance at the end of the verse governs both lines (Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David).

In the psalm's Elohistic collection the general title stands where the parallel text in Psalm 40:14 has YHWH; Ibn Ezra reads the word as placed first for emphasis, as if the line were 'God, hasten to deliver me'.

verses.translation_literal: May they be ashamed and may they blush, those seeking my life; may they be turned back backward and be humiliated, those desiring my harm.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let shame fall on them, and let the blood rise in their faces: the ones hunting my life. Let them be driven back, step by step, and left in disgrace, the ones who wish me ruin.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the first of the psalm's imprecations, and the actor should not play it as rage. In the ancient Near East shame was a public, social defeat: to be ashamed meant that your plan had failed in front of everyone who watched you make it, and that your honour went with it. So the prayer is not 'kill them' but 'let their scheme be exposed as empty'. Meiri hears it exactly so: their hope proved false, they fall from their own counsel.

The verse piles up four near synonyms, 'be ashamed', 'blush', 'be turned back', 'be humiliated', and Radak says this doubling is the usual way Hebrew intensifies. The KJV's 'confounded' for yachperu is the weaker word; it means to redden, to be abashed, and 'confusion' for yikkalemu loses the sense of humiliation in public. Notice also that 'my soul', nefesh, is not an inner spiritual essence for the Hebrew ear: it is the life, even the throat, and 'seeking my nefesh' is hunting a man to kill him. The KJV 'my soul' makes it sound like a religious quarrel.

The phrase 'turned back backward' is a deliberate doubling too: the verb sug already means 'to retreat', and the added 'achor' (backwards) makes the picture a retreat in the wrong direction, with faces still toward the one they meant to strike. Metzudat David adds that the ashamed man's instinct is to back away so no one sees his face.

philological_notes.note: Nefesh is life or throat, not only 'soul'. 'Those seeking my nefesh' is a fixed idiom for those who want to kill, which the KJV 'seek after my soul' obscures; Malbim reads it as 'to kill me'.
A verb of reddening in shame (not the homograph 'dig'). Metzudat Zion connects it with the root of 'reproach' (cherpah) by letter reversal. The pairing with yevoshu is an intensifying doublet.
Niphal of sug, 'to be turned back'; Ibn Ezra notes it is a Niphal form, like yikkonu. 'Backwards' is added for emphasis and makes the retreat a defeat.

verses.translation_literal: May they turn back on the heel of their shame, those saying, 'Aha, aha.'
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them turn and go, with their own disgrace at their heels, those who stood over me crowing, 'Aha! Aha!'
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker has heard these men. 'Aha, aha' is not a word but a sound: a gloating cry of delight at another's fall, and the actor should voice it as the enemy would, with relish, so the audience hears what the psalmist has been enduring. Rashi calls it a language of joy, in seeing an enemy as one wished. Radak's gloss is blunt: they said 'joy, joy' when I fled.

The key word is 'ekev. It is literally 'heel', and a listener would hear both meanings at once. Ibn Ezra offers the first, 'in the track, at the heels of the flock', so the men turn with their shame following behind them like a dog; Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion take the second, 'consequence, reward', as in Deuteronomy 7:12. This is the KJV's 'for a reward of their shame', which is defensible, but it hides the physical image of shame trailing at the heel. Rashi's 'measure for measure' sums up the logic of the verse: the mocking they gave will return as the mockery they receive.

philological_notes.note: Two senses are in play: 'heel, track' (Ibn Ezra's first reading, Rashi on 'in the very same path') and 'consequence, reward' (Radak, Metzudat Zion with Deut 7:12, Meiri). 'On the heel of' keeps the physical image and allows both.
An interjection of triumphant mockery, doubled for emphasis. Rashi: a language of joy at seeing an enemy as one wanted. Radak: they would say 'joy, joy' at my flight.

verses.translation_literal: May they exult and may they rejoice in you, all those seeking you; and may they say continually, 'May God be great,' those loving your salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: But let all who seek you leap for joy, and be glad in you. Let those who love your rescue say it always, without end: 'God is great! Let God be great!'
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns. The cry of 'aha' belonged to the enemies; now the psalm lifts a different cry, and the actor should let the voice open. Notice the exact contrast of vocabulary: the enemies 'seek my life' and 'desire my harm', and the righteous 'seek you' and 'love your salvation'. Same verb for seeking, opposite object. The psalm sets two crowds against each other, one hunting a man, one hunting God.

The KJV 'be magnified' is a passive rendering of the Hebrew yigdal, 'let him be great', a jussive that wishes for God's greatness to show, and the KJV makes it sound like a liturgical formula. Radak takes it plainly: God displays his greatness to those who love him and save them. 'Salvation' is yeshuah, from the same root as the name Yeshua, and for the first hearers it meant concrete rescue, not the spiritual meaning later readers put on the word. 'Continually' (tamid) is also the word for the daily offering, the 'continual' sacrifice, and may brush against that ear: a worship that never stops, like the fire on the altar.

The verse is almost word for word the end of Psalm 40. Here, though, the divine name in the last cry is Elohim, so a listener familiar with the older psalm would hear the change.

philological_notes.note: Qal jussive, 'may he be great', not a passive 'be magnified' as in the KJV. Radak explains that God shows his greatness to those who love him by saving them; Malbim says by doing ever new wonders.
'Continually, always'. It is also the word for the daily offering (the olat tamid), so an ancient hearer may catch a faint ritual echo. This echo is my own reading, not stated by the commentators.
'Your salvation', the saving act, concrete deliverance. Metzudat David glosses 'in you' (bekha) in line 1 as 'in your salvation'.

verses.translation_literal: And I [am] poor and needy; God, hasten to me. My help and my deliverer [are] you; YHWH, do not delay.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I, I am bowed and empty-handed, poor and in need. O God, come quickly to me. You are my help, you are the one who sets me free. O LORD, do not linger.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse pivots from the wish against enemies and the joy of the faithful (vv. 3–5) to the speaker himself, and the opening 'And I' sets a single bare voice against all those crowds. 'Poor and needy' ('ani ve'evyon) is not a confession of begging: it is the standard self-description of the petitioner who has no patron, no clan muscle and no legal weight, and who therefore can appeal only to the divine king as the defender of the weak. Radak ties it to David's loss of the throne; Ibn Ezra allows that the words may be what the enemies think of him, but the plain sense is the speaker's own stance. Play it quiet, almost level, with no whining.

The two commands are urgent and short. 'Chushah li' is an abrupt imperative, 'hurry to me', and the closing 'al te'achar' is its mirror, 'do not delay': the verse is framed by haste at the start and a ban on lateness at the end, and the actor should let the second line land harder than the first. The KJV's 'make no tarrying' is an archaism for 'do not delay'; 'tarry' is a word nobody uses now, and it softens the flat prohibition 'al plus the jussive into something that sounds like a polite request about waiting. Between the two cries comes the creed: 'my help and my deliverer you', with the pronoun 'attah last, so that the stress falls on who is being addressed.

philological_notes.note: A fixed pair for the poor man who has no standing, recurring in Psalms for the petitioner who looks to YHWH as his only advocate. Radak reads it of David after his son drove him from the throne; Ibn Ezra offers that it may report the enemies' opinion of him.
Imperative of 'hasten', with the ending -ah that gives it the force of a plea. Rashi glosses 'chushah li' as 'for my help' (le'ezrah), so the dative li carries the sense 'to my aid'.

'Ezri, 'my help', comes first, and mefalti, 'my deliverer' (one who lets me slip out, from palat), completes the pair. Together they say YHWH is both the one who comes to the fight and the one who brings the speaker out of it. Metzudat Zion glosses mefalti as 'a matter of rescue' (hatzalah).
'Al with the jussive is a plain prohibition, 'do not delay'. Metzudat Zion ties the verb to 'delay and appointed time'; Malbim reads it as 'do not hold back the time that salvation needs'.
